definition: The Pygmalion effect is the improvement in a person’s performance or enthusiasm that can occur when another person, such as a teacher, conveys encouragement and positive expectations. In the educational context described here, greater teacher encouragement was linked with higher student self-efficacy, stronger interest in learning, and better piano learning outcomes.

reasons: The packet supports teacher encouragement and better piano learning, but it does not directly support the broader claim that the effect occurs when a person conveys “positive expectations.”

The second sentence adds relationships that are not stated in the source, including that greater teacher encouragement was linked with higher student self-efficacy and stronger interest in learning; the packet reports correlations with enthusiasm and self-efficacy separately, not those specific paired links.

The definition states that teacher encouragement was linked with “stronger interest in learning,” but the packet reports links with “student enthusiasm in the piano course” and correlations involving self-efficacy—not specifically “interest in learning.”

The definition attributes the self-efficacy link to “the educational context described here,” but the packet describes correlations between self-efficacy and piano learning enthusiasm; the definition’s phrasing (“stronger interest in learning”) adds an element not supported by the packet.
